subtitle: Satire: mock praise, jargon taken literally, and the punchline
words.intro: German offices were among the last in the world to give up the fax machine, and some haven’t. Every town now promises a digital future. There’s a form for it, and you need to come in person to collect it. German satire has never had such an easy time.

grammar[0].blocks[2].text: *Ich will nicht ungerecht sein.* In satire, the next sentence attacks.
grammar[0].fact: Good German satire doesn’t raise its voice. It praises, and then it adds a very short sentence. *Per Post.* The shorter the sentence, the harder it hits. Notice that the writer doesn’t say a single bad word about the town. That’s also why the town can’t complain.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: Satire works best with a straight face, in the correct register. If you can write a perfect official letter, you can write this. Just change one word.
grammar[1].fact: German satire has a long legal history. *Was darf Satire?* asked Kurt Tucholsky in 1919, and answered: *Alles*. German courts have been thinking it over ever since, and sometimes they don’t agree with him.

document.intro: A real form lying on a real leaflet, for German federal employees who claim back medical costs. So here’s a German office at the digital frontier, and it has printed a leaflet to tell you about its app. Read *Bitte mit Druckbuchstaben ausfüllen*, then look at the QR code.
document.fact: German civil servants’ medical bills have their own system, *Beihilfe*, in which the state pays part. It’s a world of forms. The form says that you must not staple the receipts, and it’s not joking: *NICHT klammern*. The app, to be fair, does work.

reading.intro: Vroni has given Max a column, and he has written his first satire. It’s about the town’s new online portal. It appears on Saturday. On Tuesday there’s a letter from the town hall, by post. Here’s what he wrote, and what happened next.
reading.photos[0].caption: Ein altes Gerät: Die Behörde prüft noch, ob es zugelassen ist.
reading.fact: Germany’s plan to bring its public services online has been a slow story. A 2017 law promised nearly 600 services online by the end of 2022, and most didn’t make it. Offices in some places do still use fax, partly because it’s thought to be a safe form of delivery in law.
